snippet.title: The dark side of salmon farms | DW Documentary
snippet.description:
Salmon consumption has skyrocketed, making it one of the most popular fish across the US, Europe and Japan. To meet this huge demand, over 500 million salmon are farmed every year, accounting for around 70% of total global salmon supply. Norway dominates the industry as the world's leading producer.   

Up to 120,000 salmon are often confined within a single net-pen. Overcrowding provides ideal conditions for the rapid spread of diseases and parasites. In 2023 alone, more than 60 million farmed salmon died prematurely in Norway. The causes were severe disease outbreaks and fatal injuries suffered during aggressive treatments used to combat parasites. 

As the aquaculture industry expands, experts and activists are increasingly questioning the sustainability and ethics of these high-intensity farming methods.

This documentary is fully factual, carefully researched, and presented in a cinematic storytelling style designed to give viewers a deep, clear understanding of real-world intelligence operations without speculation or fiction. If you’re interested in geopolitics, intelligence history, secret operations, and how global power is quietly exercised, this series is for you. Watch closely — because the most important battles are the ones you never see.

snippet.title: Canada's multicultural metropolis: When night falls in Toronto | DW Documentary
snippet.description:
"We're just like New York," they say of their city, and usually add: "Only nicer!" Toronto is a melting pot of diverse cultures. Most of its residents have immigrated, at some point.

The documentary features the Neon Riders of Toronto, decorating their bikes with colorful lights and heading out at night for a ride and a party. Then there’s 28-year-old Jill, who opts to spend the night catching raccoons instead of losing herself on a club dancefloor. Or Quinn, who upholds the traditions of his Indigenous ancestors through painted constellations. And the guys from the Latino band ‘6ix Pal Mundo’, who are creating a new soundtrack for the city.
These are just a few of the many stories and moments in a film about a city that welcomes everyone, is beautiful but never pretentious, and doesn’t beg to be loved -- but is adored by its inhabitants. A place where entering the world’s largest underground pedestrian tunnel system can feel like taking a journey through several different continents.

Canada’s largest city lives up to its promise of being a thriving multicultural metropolis. Seven million people from over 230 nations live in the Greater Toronto Area. As most residents will tell you with pride, if you make the most of your opportunities, you can achieve anything here. One of the reasons why Toronto is arguably the fastest-growing city in North America. But that brings another set of problems: the number of homeless people has doubled within four years, to more than 15,000.

snippet.title: Franco’s Spain in the 1950s: How the Dictatorship Gained Legitimacy | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
In the 1950s, Spain under Francisco Franco entered a new phase known as the “Leaden Age.” After years of international isolation following World War II in 1945, the regime began to regain legitimacy. Key agreements, such as the 1953 Pact of Madrid with the United States and the 1955 admission of Spain to the United Nations, marked a turning point in Franco’s foreign policy and international standing.

These developments brought economic opportunities and a sense of stability to the country. While Spain appeared to move forward, political opposition weakened and resistance largely disappeared. Behind this controlled progress, Franco’s dictatorship remained firmly in place. This period reveals how international recognition and economic change helped secure the long-term survival of one of Europe’s most enduring authoritarian regimes.

snippet.title: Banned weapons - Why Europe is bringing back landmines | DW Documentary
snippet.description:
Landmines can maim and kill civilians and are banned in many countries under the 1997 Ottawa Treaty. Yet on Europe’s northeastern border, these controversial weapons are making a comeback.

Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Finland, Poland, and the Baltic states are rearming and bringing banned anti-personnel landmines (APLs) back into their arsenals. While military and political leaders say they contribute to strategic deterrence, mine victims and deminers say they pose a serious long-term danger. 
The war in Ukraine has reshaped Europe’s security thinking and triggered a radical shift in Finland. According to Colonel Riku Mikkonen of the Finnish armed forces, the military considers APLs a cost effective tool for national defence and a pragmatic instrument of deterrence. 
But to Zoran Ješić, who lost a leg to a mine in the Bosnian war, these weapons continue to kill, maim and render entire regions uninhabitable even decades after conflicts have ended. His story illustrates the long-term consequences of weapons that are banned by more than 160 countries.
In Helsinki, Left Alliance politician Li Andersson opposes their reintroduction and warns against a sense of Finnish exceptionalism that could undermine trust in a rules-based world order, while Green MP Atte Harjanne argues that mines are a pragmatic way to protect Finland against a Russian attack.
The documentary explores the tension between military deterrence and humanitarian consequences, asking whether anti-personnel landmines can ever be used responsibly.

snippet.title: Tracking Suspected Members of the Pakistani Taliban | Taliban Hunters (full documentary) | FRONTLINE
snippet.description:
Inside a counterterrorism police unit in Karachi, Pakistan, dedicated to tracking down suspected members of the Pakistani Taliban. (Aired 2015)

This journalism is made possible by viewers like you. Donate to FRONTLINE now: https://bit.ly/47DFzCb

And support your local PBS station here: https://www.pbs.org/donate

In the nearly five years since the Taliban seized control of Afghanistan, there’s been a dramatic increase in attacks within neighboring Pakistan by the militant group Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, commonly called the Pakistani Taliban or TTP. Pakistan has accused Taliban-controlled Afghanistan of harboring the group and enabling it to launch cross-border attacks, which the Afghan government denies — and in recent weeks, the fight between the two countries escalated into what Pakistan’s government called “open war.”

Against this volatile backdrop, FRONTLINE’s 2015 documentary “Taliban Hunters” offers relevant history on TTP and Pakistani security forces’ fight against it. This short documentary went inside a Karachi-based counterterrorism police unit dedicated to tracking down Taliban suspects. 

As the documentary reported, TTP first emerged in 2007 and used to have only a small, underground presence in Karachi, Pakistan’s largest city. But by the time the documentary aired, the group had been gaining ground in the city of over 20 million people, and carrying out suicide bombings and targeted assassinations there.

The film documented how the unit carried out raids to take suspected TTP members into custody. It also explored human rights groups’ allegations that Karachi authorities were abusing militants captured in the city’s fight against terrorism. Amid TTP’s current resurgence, “Taliban Hunters” is an illuminating snapshot of where the fight against them stood in one large city back in 2015, and how the group operated.

“Taliban Hunters” is directed and reported by Mobeen Azhar and produced by Jamie Doran. The senior producer for FRONTLINE is Dan Edge.

snippet.title: Metropolis: Carthage
snippet.description:
Discover the rise and fall of ancient Carthage—a powerful metropolis where trade, ambition, and legend shaped the Mediterranean world for centuries.

In this captivating historical documentary, journey back to the days when Carthage stood as the New York of the ancient world—a hub of commerce, innovation, and cultural exchange nestled on the North African coast. Follow the story of Margot, a merchant who faces danger and destiny on the open sea, and explore how Carthage grew from a Phoenician trading outpost into a thriving superpower whose influence drew people from across Europe, Africa, and beyond.

Learn how Carthaginian ingenuity fueled architectural marvels, cutting-edge metallurgy, and unmatched naval dominance. Delve into the daily lives of its citizens—merchants, artisans, slaves—and uncover secrets of Punic society, its unique approach to governance, and the rituals that both inspired awe and ignited controversy. See how Carthage’s wealth and strategic location attracted admiration and hatred—ultimately leading to one of the most tragic destructions in ancient history at the hands of Rome.

Through archaeological discoveries, expert interviews, and vivid storytelling, this video unveils the enduring legacy of Carthage, from the grandeur of its fabled port to the mysteries of child sacrifice and the resilience of its culture. Understand why the legend of Carthage has cast its spell across millennia and why its story still resonates today.

snippet.title: Inside Angkor Wat: The Greatest Temple Complex Ever Built | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
Hidden deep within the jungles of Cambodia stands Angkor Wat, the largest religious structure ever built and one of the greatest engineering achievements of the ancient world. Constructed during the height of the Khmer Empire in the 12th century, this vast temple complex covers more than 160 hectares and was completed in just a few decades. But how was such an enormous monument built in the middle of the jungle, and what secrets still remain hidden beneath the landscape surrounding it?

Using cutting-edge technology including satellite mapping, aerial LiDAR scans, and molecular archaeology, researchers are uncovering the lost city that once surrounded Angkor Wat and revealing the sophisticated water systems that sustained one of the world’s largest pre-industrial urban centers. This documentary explores the rise of the Khmer Empire, the spiritual meaning behind the temple’s design, and the mysteries surrounding the decline of this legendary civilization.

snippet.title: War Factories: S03 EP02
snippet.description:
Discover how factories, not just fleets, determined who won the World Wars—and how the USS Enterprise became a symbol of American might and innovation.

This video reveals the hidden engine of military victory: war production. Dive deep into why World War II was not merely a contest of naval power but a battle of factories, mass production, and industrial ingenuity. Follow the remarkable journey of the USS Enterprise, the most decorated aircraft carrier in US Navy history, from its critical role in the Pacific battles to its rapid wartime repairs—often while still under fire. Explore how the US Navy and iconic shipyards like Newport News mobilized massive workforces, including women and minorities, to outproduce Axis powers, leading to overwhelming numerical and technological advantages.

We also trace the evolution of aircraft carriers, examining pivotal moments like the battles of Midway and the Philippine Sea, and how limitations like the Washington Naval Treaty inadvertently pushed innovation forward. Japanese and US strategies, pilot training, and supply challenges are explored in detail, highlighting how logistics and shipbuilding speed played a decisive role. snippet.title: The Night Israel Almost Lost Jerusalem

snippet.title: Bombed for Four Years and Never Destroyed: The Nazi U-boat Pens of Lorient | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
Beneath the streets of London, buried inside Alpine mountains, sunk into the plains of occupied Poland, and hidden along the Atlantic coast of France, some of the most extraordinary structures of the Second World War were built in secret and never fully seen by the public. Churchill directed the war from a bunker disguised as a government basement, with a hotline to Roosevelt hidden behind a door marked "toilet." Mussolini built a 1,500-kilometre wall of Alpine fortresses partly to defend against his own ally, Hitler, while secretly storing 127 tons of Italy's national gold inside. Nazi Germany constructed a bunker line 30 metres underground that stretched over 100 kilometres along the Polish border in direct violation of Versailles. And in Lorient, France, concrete pens so thick that Allied bombing campaigns lasting four years left them completely intact while destroying 75% of the city around them. These are the bunkers that concrete built and history forgot.

snippet.title: Weapons Behind Nazi Symbols: The Rise of Nazi Germany and Mass Manipulation | Full Documentary
snippet.description:
In the year 1871, an archaeologist discovered a strange sign: a cross with angled arms. He has no idea that in a few years this cross will become a symbol under the name Swastika - for hatred, destruction, and the Holocaust. Hitler himself will claim to have designed the symbol. snippet.title: Nikola Tesla - The visionary who invented our future | DW Documentary
snippet.description:
Nikola Tesla, born in 1856 in what is now Croatia, was one of the world’s greatest inventors. He developed numerous innovations in the field of electrical engineering and was granted over 280 patents, many of them in the USA.

Nikola Tesla arrived in New York in 1884 with barely a cent to his name. He worked briefly for Thomas Alva Edison, the inventor of the light bulb. However, their collaboration soon ended in a dispute. In the years that followed, Tesla developed groundbreaking technologies and implemented alternating current systems for the Westinghouse company. These shaped modern electrification.

For decades, Tesla conducted research into high-frequency alternating currents and the vision of wireless power transmission - a concept that was far ahead of its time. He also recognized early on that solar energy would become one of the most important sources of energy in the future. However, his visionary inventions were not fully realized during his lifetime.

Tesla’s life was marked by extremes: periods of abject poverty and professional setbacks alternated with an eccentric lifestyle that’s been heavily mythologized. In 1943, he died alone and destitute in a New York hotel.
